title: Random Variables, Kernels, and Fubini
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter answers two questions that undergraduate probability leaves informal. First: given a target distribution $\nu$, can we always build an actual random variable with that distribution, and can we build many independent ones -- or even a whole infinite sequence -- out of a single source of randomness? Second: what precisely *is* the "conditional distribution of $X_2$ given $X_1 = s_1$" as a mathematical object, when $X_1$ need not be discrete and need not have a density? It assumes the measure-theoretic setup of probability spaces, measurable spaces and product $\sigma$-algebras, the $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem, monotone convergence, and Radon-Nikodym derivatives. ## Constructing a random variable with a prescribed distribution A random variable $X$ taking values in a measurable space $(S,\mathcal S)$ has a distribution $\nu$, $$\nu(A) = P(X\in A),\qquad A\in\mathcal S.$$ Turn this around: given a probability measure $\nu$ on $(S,\mathcal S)$, does some random variable have distribution $\nu$? There is a trivial answer -- take $\Omega = S$ and let $X$ be the identity map -- but it says nothing about how $X$ sits inside a richer probability space alongside other random variables. The useful question is whether $X$ can be built as a measurable function of a *fixed*, simple source of randomness: a uniform random variable $U$ on $(0,1)$. ### The quantile transform Recall the one-dimensional device from an undergraduate course. **Lemma 1.** Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with distribution function $F(x) = \mu(-\infty,x]$, and let $$F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x)\ge u\},\qquad 0\le u\le 1$$ be its inverse. If $U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, then $F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution $\mu$. This is the reason simulation software only ever needs one random number generator: any real-valued distribution is a fixed function of a uniform. ### Beyond the real line To push this past $\mathbb R$, replace $F^{-1}$ by any measurable $h$. **Lemma 2.** Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on a *nice* space $S$ -- meaning $S$ is Standard Borel: there is a measurable bijection $\phi: S\to\mathbb R$ with measurable inverse. Then there is a measurable $h:[0,1]\to S$ such that $h(U)$ has distribution $\nu$. *Argument.* Push $\nu$ forward through $\phi$ to get a measure on $\mathbb R$, apply Lemma 1 to get $F^{-1}$, then set $h = \phi^{-1}\circ F^{-1}$. "Nice" is not exotic: every complete separable metric space is Standard Borel, so Lemma 2 covers essentially every space encountered in practice. ### Collapsing many random variables into one uniform Apply Lemma 2 with $S=\mathbb R^\infty$ and $\nu$ = the joint law of a whole sequence $(X_1,X_2,\dots)$: **Corollary 3.** For any sequence of real-valued random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ there exist measurable functions $h_1,h_2,\dots$ such that $(h_1(U),h_2(U),\dots)$ has the same joint distribution as $(X_1,X_2,\dots)$. *Argument.* Treat $\mathbf X=(X_1,X_2,\dots)$ as a single $\mathbb R^\infty$-valued random variable and apply Lemma 2. This is worth pausing on, because it is genuinely counter-intuitive: however large or dependent the sequence $(X_1,X_2,\dots)$, all of its randomness can be squeezed out of one uniform random variable on $(0,1)$ -- no extra source of randomness is ever needed, only a more complicated function of the one you have. ### An explicit construction: splitting the bits of $U$ Lemma 2 is an existence statement; here is a hands-on construction that also produces *independence*. Write the binary expansion of $U$, $$U = \sum_{i=1}^\infty B_i 2^{-i},$$ where the bits $B_1,B_2,\dots$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Fix disjoint infinite sets of indices $I^{(1)}, I^{(2)},\dots$, say $I^{(k)} = (i_{k1},i_{k2},\dots)$, and reassemble a new uniform from each block: $$U_k = \sum_{j=1}^\infty B_{i_{kj}}\, 2^{-j}.$$ Because the blocks $I^{(k)}$ are disjoint, the bits feeding $U_1, U_2,\dots$ are disjoint subsets of the same independent sequence $(B_i)$, so $U_1,U_2,\dots$ are themselves independent, each Uniform$(0,1)$. Feeding these through Lemma 1 gives: **Corollary 4.** For any probability measures $\theta_1,\theta_2,\dots$ on $\mathbb R$ there exist independent random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $X_i\sim\theta_i$. Notice what this proof did *not* use: the Kolmogorov extension theorem, which is the usual tool for patching a consistent family of finite-dimensional distributions into an infinite one. The construction here is more concrete -- it builds the whole sequence directly out of the bits of one uniform. (The lecture notes at this point point onward to Radon-Nikodym densities before turning to conditioning -- see Sources.) ## Conditional distributions as probability kernels ### The object being formalized Undergraduate probability writes the conditional distribution of $X_2$ given $X_1=s_1$ using densities, $f(x,y)=f(x)f(y\mid x)$. That formula presupposes the joint law has a density. The measure-theoretic question is what kind of object $$Q(s_1,B) = P(X_2\in B\mid X_1=s_1)$$ is when it does not. **Definition.** Let $(S_1,\mathcal S_1)$ and $(S_2,\mathcal S_2)$ be measurable spaces. A *kernel* $Q$ from $S_1$ to $S_2$ is a map $Q: S_1\times\mathcal S_2\to\mathbb R$ such that (a) $B\mapsto Q(s_1,B)$ is a probability measure on $(S_2,\mathcal S_2)$, for each fixed $s_1$; (b) $s_1\mapsto Q(s_1,B)$ is measurable, for each fixed $B\in\mathcal S_2$. If $S_1$ and $S_2$ are countable, a kernel is exactly a stochastic matrix -- row $s_1$ is the conditional distribution given $X_1=s_1$. This is the general version of that idea: (a) says every "row" is a genuine probability measure; (b) says the "matrix" varies measurably across rows, so that averaging over $s_1$ makes sense. ### What it means for $Q$ to be *the* conditional kernel of $\mu$ Given a joint law $\mu$ on $S_1\times S_2$ and its $S_1$-marginal $\mu_1$, a kernel $Q$ deserves to be called the conditional distribution of the second coordinate given the first when it disintegrates $\mu$ correctly. There are three equivalent ways to say this. **Proposition 5.** The following are equivalent, for a probability measure $\mu$ on $S_1\times S_2$, a probability measure $\mu_1$ on $S_1$, and a kernel $Q$ from $S_1$ to $S_2$: $$\mu(A\times B) = \int_A Q(s,B)\,\mu_1(ds), \qquad A\in\mathcal S_1,\ B\in\mathcal S_2; \tag{1}$$ $$\mu(D) = \int_{S_1} Q(s_1, D_{s_1})\,\mu_1(ds_1), \qquad D\in\mathcal S_1\times\mathcal S_2, \tag{2}$$ where $D_{s_1}=\{s_2:(s_1,s_2)\in D\}$ is the slice of $D$ above $s_1$; and $$\int_{S_1\times S_2} h\,d\mu = \int_{S_1}\left(\int_{S_2} h(s_1,s_2)\,Q(s_1,ds_2)\right)\mu_1(ds_1) \tag{3}$$ for every measurable $h\ge0$ (or every $\mu$-integrable $h$). Both the meaningfulness of (2) and the proof rest on a measurability fact about slices: **Lemma 6.** For every $D\in\mathcal S_1\times\mathcal S_2$: (i) $D_{s_1}\in\mathcal S_2$ for every $s_1$; (ii) $s_1\mapsto Q(s_1,D_{s_1})$ is measurable. (Proved by applying the $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem to the class of sets $D$ for which (i)-(ii) hold: true for rectangles, and the class is a $\lambda$-system.) *Why (1), (2), (3) are equivalent.* $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: (2) is meaningful by Lemma 6; it holds for rectangles $D=A\times B$ by (1), and the class of $D$ for which it holds is a $\lambda$-system containing the $\pi$-system of rectangles, so it holds for all $D$ by the $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem. $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$: (3) is (2) when $h=1_D$; extend to simple $h$ by linearity, to $h\ge0$ by writing $h$ as an increasing limit of simple functions and invoking monotone convergence, and to general $h$ by splitting $h=h^+-h^-$. Call $Q$ *the conditional probability kernel* for $\mu$ (non-standard terminology, but descriptive): it is the object that plays the role of "$P(X_2\in\cdot\mid X_1=s_1)$" rigorously. ### Existence: the easy direction and the hard one **Theorem 7.** *Easy part.* Given a probability measure $\mu_1$ on $S_1$ and a kernel $Q$ from $S_1$ to $S_2$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $S_1\times S_2$ satisfying (1)-(3). *Hard part.* Conversely, given $\mu$ on $S_1\times S_2$ with marginal $\mu_1(A)=\mu(A\times S_2)$, if $S_2$ is nice then a kernel $Q$ satisfying (1)-(3) exists. The easy part runs Proposition 5 in reverse: define $\mu$ by formula (2), which makes sense because of Lemma 6, and check countable additivity by monotone convergence along $D^n\uparrow D$. The content of the theorem -- and the reason regular conditional distributions are not automatic -- is the hard part: a joint law always determines a marginal, but recovering a genuine kernel (one probability measure per value of $s_1$, varying measurably) from the joint law is a real construction, and it needs a niceness hypothesis on $S_2$. ### How the hard part is built As with Lemma 2, reduce to $S_2=\mathbb R$ by transporting through the bijection $\phi$; write $S_1=S$. For each rational $r$, let $\nu_r$ be the sub-probability measure on $S$ $$\nu_r(A) = \mu(A\times(-\infty,r]),$$ which satisfies $\nu_r\le\mu_1$ and so has a Radon-Nikodym density $F(s,r)=d\nu_r/d\mu_1$ -- measurable in $s$ for each fixed $r$, but only defined up to a $\mu_1$-null set that depends on $r$. The obstacle is that "null" depends on $r$, and a different bad set of $s$'s could in principle appear for every rational $r$. The fix is that there are only *countably* many rationals, so only countably many null sets are ever in play, and their union is still null. Modify $F$ on that one countable union so that, simultaneously for every remaining $s$, $r\mapsto F(s,r)$ is non-decreasing (from $F(s,r_2)-F(s,r_1)\ge0$ a.e. for $r_1 ### Worked example: Parseval's identity Let $X\sim\mu$ have characteristic function $\phi(t)=E\exp(itX)$ and let $Y\sim\nu$ have characteristic function $\hat\phi(t)$. Compute $E\exp(iXY)$ two ways -- integrating out $Y$ first, or $X$ first -- and Fubini gives $$\int \phi(t)\,\nu(dt) = \int \hat\phi(t)\,\mu(dt).$$ ### Worked example: convolution beyond densities If $X\sim\mu$ and $Y$ are independent and $S=X+Y$, the undergraduate convolution formula for densities is $$f_S(s) = \int f_Y(s-x)\,f_X(x)\,dx,$$ which presupposes both $X$ and $Y$ have densities. The fully general statement, in terms of distribution functions, needs no densities at all: $$F_S(s) = \int F_Y(s-x)\,\mu(dx).$$ If only $Y$ happens to have a density $f_Y$, this sharpens to $$f_S(s) = \int f_Y(s-x)\,\mu(dx),$$ with no assumption that $X$ has a density either.
